title: American brands you should know
summary: About 95 household US brands across eight categories, each with its parent and a one-phrase positioning. Interviewers use these names as shorthand for business models, so recognising them instantly saves time and credibility.

blocks.title: How to use this list
blocks.body: Interviewers drop brand names without explanation: 'think of a Chipotle-like chain' or 'a client like Clorox.' You need the one-phrase positioning and, often, the parent company, because portfolio and channel questions hinge on it. These tables cover the brands most likely to come up. Learn the positioning, not the trivia; in a case, a brand is shorthand for a business model.

blocks.title: Parents changed recently
blocks.body: Ownership moves fast: Mars bought Kellanova (Pringles, Cheez-It) in 2025, Ferrero bought WK Kellogg (US cereal), Capital One bought Discover, and Walgreens went private. Southwest dropped free bags and open seating. If unsure of a parent, say so and reason from the business model rather than guessing.

in_a_case: 'Our client is a Clorox-type CPG company': think branded consumables, big-box customers (Walmart, Costco), private label threat.
A QSR growth case: know franchise vs company-operated (McDonald's franchises; Starbucks mostly operates its own US stores).
Payments cases: separate networks (Visa, Mastercard) from issuers (Chase, Capital One) and wallets (PayPal, Cash App).
Fit and small talk: brands from recent experience (Trader Joe's, Chipotle, Costco runs) are safe, relatable examples.
Brainstorming competitors or partners: name the right US players (DoorDash, Instacart, Uber Eats) instead of Indian equivalents.
